title: Hornbill: The Voice of the Rain (poem)

topics.title: Whitman asks the rain, 'Who are you?'

learn.hook: What if you asked the monsoon who it was, and it answered? Walt Whitman's poem is exactly that conversation.
points: Walt Whitman was an American poet, often called the father of free verse; his famous collection is 'Leaves of Grass'.
'The Voice of the Rain' is a dialogue poem: the poet asks the soft-falling shower who it is, and the rain replies.
The poet asks, in old-fashioned words, 'And who art thou?' and the rain answers that it is the Poem of Earth.
Two voices: the poet (the opening question and the bracketed lines at the end) and the rain (the long answer in between).
'As here translated': the poet claims to translate the rain's answer into human words.

example.q: Identify the two voices in the poem.
steps: The poet speaks first, asking the shower who it is.
The rain replies, describing itself as the Poem of Earth and its journey.
The bracketed lines at the end are the poet's comment.
example.answer: The poet (question and bracketed lines) and the rain (the reply in between).

learn.reallife: Every June, Kerala welcomes the monsoon as if it were a guest. Whitman goes one step further and lets the rain introduce itself.

learn.hook: Evaporation, condensation, precipitation: you learnt them in Class 6 science. Whitman puts the same cycle into the rain's own mouth.
points: The rain rises unseen ('impalpable', not able to be touched) from the land and the bottomless sea, upward to the sky: evaporation.
In the sky it is vaguely formed, altogether changed, and yet the same: condensation into clouds.
It descends to wash ('lave') the droughts, the tiny particles ('atomies') and the dust-layers of the globe: precipitation.
The cycle repeats: water rises, changes form, falls and returns to its source.
The rain stays the same substance even though its form changes: vapour, cloud, drop.

example.q: Explain the water cycle as shown in the poem.
steps: Evaporation: rain rises unseen from land and sea.
Condensation: it changes form in the sky, yet stays the same.
Precipitation: it falls to wash the droughts and dust of the earth.
Return: it gives back life to its origin.
example.answer: Rain rises as vapour, forms clouds, falls as rain on dry land and returns to its source, again and again.

learn.reallife: IMD tracks this very cycle: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal moisture rises, forms monsoon clouds over the Western Ghats, and falls on fields across India.

steps: A: the poem describes the water cycle – true.

learn.hook: A seed can lie in the soil for months waiting. One shower, and it cracks open. Whitman's rain knows its power.
points: Without rain, seeds would remain only seeds: latent (hidden, inactive) and unborn.
Rain gives back life to its own origin: the earth and sea from which it rose.
It makes the earth pure and beautiful, by day and by night, forever.
Rain gives selflessly: it asks for nothing and returns again and again.
'Strange to tell': surprisingly, the rain gave an answer. The phrase marks the wonder of a shower speaking.

example.q: What is meant by 'strange to tell'?
steps: Rain is not expected to speak.
Yet it answers the poet.
So the poet calls it strange, a wonder worth telling.
example.answer: It means 'surprisingly', since it is strange that the rain could reply.

learn.reallife: Indian farmers watch the first monsoon showers before sowing kharif crops; without rain, the seeds in the soil remain latent, exactly as the poem says.

topics.title: Rain and song: the bracketed lines

learn.hook: A song leaves a singer's heart, travels to listeners who may or may not care, and still comes back with love. Whitman says rain does the same.
points: The last two lines, in brackets, compare rain to a song.
A song issues from its birthplace (the poet's heart), wanders, is heard or ignored ('reck'd or unreck'd'), and duly returns with love.
Analogy: rain rises from the earth and returns to it; poetry or music rises from the poet and returns to bless the world.
Metaphor: rain as the Poem of Earth; simile-like comparison: rain is like a song.
Why brackets? They mark the poet's own comment, set apart from the rain's voice.

example.q: What analogy does the poem draw between rain and music?
steps: Rain: rises from earth and sea, falls back to give life.
Song: rises from the poet's heart, reaches the world, returns with love.
Both complete a cycle and give without demanding.
example.answer: Both rise from a source, travel, enrich others and return to their origin, whether noticed or not.

learn.reallife: A song by Lata Mangeshkar or A.R. Rahman leaves the studio, travels everywhere, and returns as love from listeners. That is the bracketed lines' idea.

topics.title: Devices: personification, archaic words, free verse

learn.hook: Rain that speaks, words like 'thou' and 'art', and lines that refuse to rhyme: Whitman's poem is full of tools examiners love.
points: Personification: the rain speaks and describes its own journey.
Archaic language: thou (you), art (are), reck'd/unreck'd (heeded/unheeded), lave (wash), drouths (droughts), atomies (tiny particles).
Free verse: no fixed rhyme or metre; inversion of normal word order (e.g., 'said I' for 'I said').
Parentheses (brackets) set apart the poet's closing comment.
Alliteration and imagery: 'said I to the soft-falling shower' repeats the s sound; 'bottomless sea' and 'dust-layers of the globe' give vivid pictures.

example.q: Find an inversion in the poem and rewrite it in normal order.
steps: Inversion: 'said I to the soft-falling shower'.
Normal order puts subject before verb.
Rewrite: 'I said to the soft-falling shower'.

learn.reallife: Old Hindi film songs and bhajans often use poetic inversion and old words; poets choose them to sound timeless, as Whitman did.

remember: Archaic words give a timeless, solemn tone
traps: The poem is free verse, not rhyming couplets

learn.hook: Rain has inspired poets everywhere, from Kalidasa's 'Meghaduta', with a cloud as messenger, to Tagore's monsoon songs. Comparing poems is a great way to see what makes Whitman's special.
points: Try this out: find other poems on rain and compare their mood, imagery and message with Whitman's.
Kalidasa's 'Meghaduta' uses a cloud as a messenger; Tagore wrote many songs of the monsoon. Whitman's rain is a voice and a poet.
Extract questions often test: the water cycle, personification, the meaning of 'strange to tell', and the bracketed lines.
When comparing poems, look at speaker, imagery, devices and theme.

example.q: Compare: In one poem rain is a destroyer (floods); in Whitman's it is a life-giver. What is the key difference?
steps: Identify the role of rain in each.
Whitman: gives life and beauty, returns to its origin.
Other: brings danger and loss.
example.answer: Whitman celebrates rain as a selfless creator; the other poem shows its destructive side.

learn.reallife: In Indian languages there are countless monsoon songs, such as Hindi 'barkha' songs. Comparing them with Whitman shows rain's many faces.
